summary: An April 1 RFC and a humorous one. It claims to solve the Y10K problem, which comes from the year 10000 needing five digits instead of four, along with tongue-in-cheek variants named for hexadecimal and Roman numerals. It is informational, not a real standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke about what happens when years have five digits, like the year 10000. It was published on April Fools' Day.

subtitle: A humorous proposal to solve the year 10,000 date crisis.

tldr.problem: Fixing the Y2K problem by using 4-digit years creates a new crisis: all those programs will fail again in the year 10,000 when 4 digits are no longer enough. The RFC parodies how the same short-term thinking that created Y2K will inevitably create Y10K.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a solution that uses letters and carets as prefixes to extend the year representation arbitrarily far into the future, allowing lexical sorting of dates regardless of their precision or the century they fall in.
tldr.outcome: This April 1st joke demonstrates that any fixed date format will eventually fail and that future-proofing requires thinking beyond the next few decades.

today: RFC 2550 is an Informational RFC published on 1 April 1999, marked as a joke. It remains unobsoleted and is famous in RFC circles as a humorous commentary on the cyclical nature of date representation problems.

sections.title: The Y10K Problem
sections.content: This April 1st RFC humorously points out that the Y2K fix creates a new problem. Most Y2K solutions switched from 2-digit years to 4-digit years, extending the working date range from the year 2000 to 9999. However, this is exactly the flawed thinking that caused Y2K: assuming current code will not outlive its intended lifespan. When the year 10,000 arrives, all those 4-digit year systems will fail.
sections.plainLanguage: People fixed the year 2000 problem by using bigger numbers, but that fix stops working in the year 10000. It is funny because people made the same mistake again.

sections.title: An Extensible Date Format
sections.content: The RFC proposes a format that handles arbitrarily large years. For years 1 through 9999, use the traditional 4-digit format. For years 10,000 to 99,999, prepend the letter 'A' to a 5-digit year. For years 100,000 and beyond, use letters B, C, and so on. This scheme allows dates to sort correctly lexically and extend indefinitely into the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of just using bigger numbers forever, the format adds letters before huge numbers so they still sort in the right order. Year 10000 becomes A10000, and it comes after 9999 when you sort alphabetically.

sections.title: Future-Proof Date Handling
sections.content: The format uses a layering scheme: dates with 5-digit years begin with 'A', those with 6-digit years with 'B', and so forth, covering all years up to 10 to the power of 30. For even larger years, the RFC extends the system using multiple carets and a base-26 encoding scheme. It emphasizes that any solution must support arbitrary precision and extensibility, since even the expected lifetime of the universe (10 to the power of 11 years) is not infinite.
sections.plainLanguage: The solution keeps adding new letters and special characters for bigger and bigger numbers, so no matter how far into the future we go, the dates still sort correctly and work the same way.
